⚡️ Army chief praises Basij contributions to Iran’s security, public service 📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran’s Army Chief Major General Amir Hatami praises the Basij Organization for its role in critical moments, saying the volunteer force has demonstrated commitment through defense, relief work, and social services. In a message marking Basij Week, Hatami described the organization as a lasting strategic initiative of the late Imam Khomeini and a force rooted in public faith and resolve to safeguard Iran’s independence, security, and dignity. ​ He said the Basij had played an effective role in the Sacred Defense during the war imposed by the Iraqi Ba’ath regime, countering threats, helping disadvantaged communities, reconstruction, emergency response, scientific and cultural activities, and protecting public security. ​ Hatami said this record showed that the Basij was more than an organization; it represented a culture of faith, people-oriented values, responsibility, and self-sacrifice. ​ This year’s Basij Week slogan, “Basij: Devoted to the People, Hope for the Underprivileged,” reflected its close ties with the public, he said. The force had stood alongside people during difficult circumstances, including natural disasters and service campaigns. Public trust, he added, was its greatest source of strength. ​ Referring to the recent war, Hatami said Basij members had stood alongside other Armed Forces and the public in confronting complex threats to Iran’s independence, security, and territorial integrity. Their presence, he said, demonstrated the force’s capacity and public readiness to defend the country. ​ Hatami concluded by honoring Basij members killed in service and congratulating its members, veterans, families of martyrs, and the Iranian people on Basij Week, and praised their continued service to Iran. 📲 @Irna_en ​

🌟 85 years ago, on November 22, 1941, Military Motor Road No. 101 opened across the frozen waters of Lake Ladoga, connecting besieged Leningrad with the mainland and going down in history as the legendary Road of Life . By that time, Leningrad had already been encircled by enemy forces for nearly three months. On September 8, 1941, following the capture of Shlisselburg by Nazi troops, the city's overland connections with the rest of the country were severed. More than 2.5 million civilians, including 400,000 children , as well as the troops of the Leningrad Front, found themselves trapped in the besieged city. The city endured relentless artillery shelling and air raids. But the most terrible ordeal was hunger. On November 20, daily bread rations were reduced to a devastating 250 grammes for workers and just 125 grammes for office workers, dependants and children. 🕯 According to various estimates , between 800,000 and 1 million people died of starvation in Leningrad (more than the combined losses of the United States and Britain throughout the Second World War). Not a single household was spared the tragedy .* *In 2026, April 19 was designated in Russia as the Day of Remembrance for the Victims of the Genocide of the Soviet People , perpetrated by the Nazis and their accomplices during the Great Patriotic War. *** 🧊 Lake Ladoga remained the only route for supplying besieged Leningrad with food and ammunition, as well as evacuating civilians. Since September, supplies had been transported across the lake by water, but with winter approaching, even this vital lifeline was at risk of being cut off. The solution was an ice road approximately 30 kilometres long. It was prepared in record time, despite harsh weather conditions and the danger of vehicles breaking through the ice, which had yet to reach sufficient thickness. On November 20, the first horse-drawn convoy of 350 sledges crossed Lake Ladoga, delivering 63 tonnes of flour. On the evening of November 21, ten GAZ-AA trucks made a trial run. 🚚 On November 22, motor vehicle traffic began along the Road of Life. The first large-scale convoy consisted of 60 legendary GAZ-AA trucks , affectionately known as polutorkas (one-and-a-half-tonners), carrying life-saving supplies for the starving city. Every journey was an act of heroism. Drivers worked amid bitter frosts , constant enemy air raids and artillery shelling , and attacks by enemy landing forces . Thousands of people kept the road operational – drivers, military engineers, road workers, mechanics and loaders. All of them risked their lives every day to save Leningrad. 📊 During the first winter of the siege, in 1941-1942 , the ice road carried 361,000 tonnes of supplies into the city, including 262,000 tonnes of food, while 550,000 people were evacuated. Over the entire period of the Road of Life's operation (until March 1943), including both waterborne and ice-road transport, more than 1.6 million tonnes of supplies were delivered to Leningrad
